agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: The gap holds across all 116 pairs: "####" at the end of a reference solution has median logprob −6.8 in eval chat format against −2.9 raw, and a quarter of v0 cases fall below −10. So in exactly the format where the user asks for "#### <number>", the marker is suppressed by about 4 nats. Whether this matters depends on grading. Without a marker, the grader takes the last number, which can be wrong if the answer is followed by other numbers, or if the model never commits to an answer. Before trying to localize the suppression, I'll estimate the accuracy at stake from the existing generations (gen_21 original and E4). I'll count marker use, and among wrong answers without a marker, how often the gold number still appears in the final lines. If many unmarked wrong answers contain the gold near the end, marker suppression costs real points and is worth localizing. If very few do, it's cosmetic, and loops and reasoning errors are the real target.

The marker turns out to be a sign of failure. In the original generations, answers that use "####" are correct only 7.6% of the time, against 22.6% for answers without it. The same holds under E4 (9% vs 24%). Unmarked wrong answers rarely have the gold number at the end (6 of 81), so the missing marker isn't costing points through grading. The surprising part is how bad the marked answers are. Perhaps when the model does produce "####", it does so early, as a guess, or the marker comes with a wrong or degraded final step. I'll profile the marked answers in gen_21_original (token counts, where the marker falls, cut or not) and quote the start and end of two short ones. If marked answers are short early guesses, the model may be routing to a "give a quick wrong answer" mode, a candidate sabotage behaviour to localize. If they are long and ordinary, the 7.6% is a quirk and I move on.

The marked answers are short (median 159 tokens against 254) and never cut. Their errors are semantic: adding chairs to round tables to get "legs", an invented $5 price, an extra doubling. So the marker is not itself the target, and the reasoning damage looks the same as elsewhere. I'm closing the marker line, since the suppression is real but grading-neutral. The best causal handle remains L11 head 3 → gate neurons. E4 removes only the two strongest, and the gate signal may be spread over more units that head 3 drives specifically in eval-format math. fwd_18 (original) and fwd_19 (head 3 zeroed) cover the same texts at layers 11–13. For each neuron I'll compute how much the head-3 ablation changes its response-mean activation in v0 (eval math) against the controls (v3 raw math, non-math chat), and list neurons with large, v0-specific head-3 dependence. A set of further units with clearly v0-specific dependence would give a principled "E4+" candidate: the same mechanism, a wider cut. If only 6176/6508 (and their L12 followers) show up, the gate really is two neurons and the remaining deficit is elsewhere.

Beyond 6176 and 6508, layer 11 contains a second tier of neurons that depend on head 3 mainly in eval-format math: 3585 (Δ −0.66), 848 (−0.58), 3704 (−0.50), 2377 (+0.40), 4960 (−0.30), 4739 (+0.19). For each, the head-3 dependence in raw math and in non-math chat is small (|Δ| < 0.2). Their effects, weighted by write size, are about a quarter of 6176's each. Together they could carry a sizeable part of the gate signal that E4 leaves behind, which would fit E4's partial recovery. Before building an edit, I'll check that each also has the AND signature in the original model. Its v0 level should differ clearly from both v3 and chat, so that zeroing its write moves eval-math toward the controls and doesn't remove a constant everywhere. Units that pass will form E8, E4 plus those columns zeroed. A unit whose v0 level matches the controls (only its head-3 source differs) would be excluded.
